content: Psychological therapy and counseling for patients with mental health and/or substance use comorbidities have been shown to significantly increase the initiation and completion of hepatitis C virus (HCV) treatment. These interventions also lead to higher sustained virologic response (SVR) rates. Integrating services for specific populations, such as people who inject drugs, may further enhance the effectiveness of HCV care. The Guidelines Development Group reviewed evidence from recent systematic reviews on interventions aimed at improving linkage to care following HIV testing. These findings were deemed relevant to hepatitis care and treatment services. Education and support for peer and lay health care workers were identified as critical components in strengthening service delivery, particularly in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Lay health workers have been shown to effectively perform interventions typically carried out by trained medical personnel, thereby supporting the decentralization of services and non-facility-based testing. Peer-led interventions were found to be feasible, acceptable, and cost-effective, making them particularly suitable for resource-limited settings. Clinician reminders align with broader efforts to standardize clinical practice, including provider-initiated screening and systems-based approaches to improve clinical outcomes. These reminders are relatively easy to implement and have proven effective in other disease modalities, such as breast and colorectal cancer screening. Integrating HCV screening and treatment with mental health and substance use services is both feasible and acceptable to targeted clients. Co-location and coordination of services appear to be key contributors to improved outcomes in multidisciplinary or integrated care models. Although no direct cost or cost-effectiveness estimates were reported in the systematic review, effective linkage to hepatitis care and treatment following a positive diagnosis is expected to enhance program efficiency. This includes earlier treatment initiation, reduced loss to follow-up, and cost savings across the care continuum. Proactive linkage approaches are essential for comprehensive hepatitis testing services. Countries should implement specific policies and strategies to improve and prioritize linkages between hepatitis testing, prevention, treatment, and care services. Strengthening multiple steps along the care continuum is likely to yield the most efficient outcomes. Monitoring linkage following hepatitis testing is critical to improving treatment and prevention cascades. Success should be measured by enrollment in care rather than intermediate indicators, such as the number of referrals issued. The updated WHO Consolidated Guidelines on HIV, viral hepatitis, and sexually transmitted infection (STI) prevention, diagnosis, treatment, and care for key populations, published in July 2022, include new recommendations. These include the use of peer navigators to support individuals from key populations in initiating and remaining in treatment, as well as offering online delivery of services as an additional option. HCV diagnostics rely on the detection of antibodies to determine current or past infection and to triage individuals for further evaluation of active viral replication. Between 15–45% of individuals infected with HCV will spontaneously clear the infection but remain HCV antibody-positive while being HCV RNA-negative. Diagnosis of viremic HCV infection in antibody-positive individuals distinguishes those requiring treatment from those who have cleared the infection. The preferred strategy for diagnosing viremic HCV infection is nucleic acid testing (NAT) for HCV RNA, either quantitative or qualitative. HCV core antigen assays, which have comparable sensitivity to laboratory-based NAT, can serve as an alternative diagnostic approach. Point-of-care (POC) HCV RNA NAT assays are also recommended as an alternative to laboratory-based NAT, particularly in resource-limited settings, due to their potential for lower cost and accessibility. Laboratory-based NAT technologies are highly sensitive and specific but require sophisticated equipment and skilled personnel. POC NAT assays, which are now commercially available, offer a decentralized and potentially more cost-effective option. A systematic review and meta-analysis demonstrated that POC HCV RNA testing increases the uptake of testing and treatment initiation while reducing the time to results and treatment initiation compared to laboratory-based approaches. The diagnostic accuracy of POC HCV RNA NAT assays is high, with pooled sensitivity and specificity of 99% relative to laboratory-based reference standards. These assays have shown consistent performance across various settings, populations, and specimen types. WHO has previously recommended POC NAT molecular assays for the rapid diagnosis of other diseases, such as tuberculosis (TB) and HIV. The expansion of POC diagnostic options for HCV represents a significant advancement in improving access to care, particularly in LMICs.
